title: Archimedes' principle and floating equilibrium

learning_outcomes.text: understand that the upthrust acting on an object in a fluid is due to a difference in hydrostatic pressure
calculate the upthrust acting on an object in a fluid using the equation F = ρgV (Archimedes' principle)

prior_knowledge_summary: A fluid can exert a larger pressure force on the bottom of an immersed object than on its top.
Appropriate sideways pressure forces cancel, leaving an upward resultant called upthrust.
An object in equilibrium has zero resultant force.
Weight is calculated using W = mg, and the volume of a uniform prism is cross-sectional area multiplied by length.
new_learning: Calculate upthrust from fluid density, gravitational field strength and displaced volume.
Choose the displaced volume correctly for fully and partly immersed objects.
Set upthrust equal to weight for an object floating freely in equilibrium.
Relate the fraction submerged to the densities of an object and its fluid.
not_yet_taught: Buoyancy stability, centres of buoyancy and metacentres

visual_planning.reason: Six different visual forms support the pressure origin, displaced volume, calculation routine, equilibrium, misconception correction and final synthesis. Assets were not requested in this text-package run.

blocks.heading: How much water must move out of the way?
content: A sealed lunch box is pushed completely under water. You push it deeper without tilting or crushing it. Does the upthrust become larger just because the box is deeper?
The pressure around it is larger at the greater depth, but the difference between the pressure forces on its bottom and top is unchanged when the water density and the box dimensions stay the same.
The useful clue is not depth by itself. It is the amount of fluid the box displaces.

figure.purpose: Create a depth-versus-displaced-volume prediction without revealing the conclusion visually.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch with the same sealed box shown fully submerged at a shallow and deeper position in a tank. Keep box size and water uniform. Add sparse pressure arrows and a question mark between the two states. Do not label either upthrust as larger or equal.
figure.alt_text: The same sealed box is shown fully submerged at two different depths in uniform water.

blocks.heading: The displaced fluid gives the upthrust
content: Lesson 10 explained upthrust as the upward resultant of pressure forces. Archimedes' principle gives a shorter calculation route: the upthrust equals the weight of the fluid displaced by the object.
The formula to remember is F = ρgV. For a completely submerged rigid object, V is the whole object volume. For a floating or partly immersed object, V is only the volume below the fluid surface.
A block of volume 0.018 m³ is fully submerged in sea water of density 1020 kg m⁻³. Its upthrust is F = (1020)(9.81)(0.018) = 180.1 N, or 180 N to three significant figures. The force is upward.

symbols: F is the upthrust in newtons, N.
ρ is the density of the displaced fluid in kilograms per cubic metre, kg m⁻³.
g is the gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram, N kg⁻¹.
V is the volume of fluid displaced in cubic metres, m³.
formula_to_remember.units: Using kg m⁻³, N kg⁻¹ and m³ gives newtons.

figure.purpose: Connect an immersed object's shape to an equal displaced-fluid volume and its weight.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper three-panel sequence: object entering water, highlighted submerged volume, then the same-shaped volume of displaced fluid on a simple balance labelled mass rho V and weight rho g V. Finish with one upward arrow F on the object.
figure.alt_text: The submerged volume is matched to an equal volume of displaced fluid whose weight gives the upthrust.

blocks.heading: Choose V before substituting
content: A vertical cylinder has cross-sectional area 0.030 m². Only 0.12 m of its height is below the surface of oil of density 850 kg m⁻³.
The displaced volume is not the whole cylinder volume. It is V = Ah = (0.030)(0.12) = 3.6 × 10⁻³ m³.
Now use Archimedes' principle: F = ρgV = (850)(9.81)(3.6 × 10⁻³) = 30.0 N upward. A unit check gives (kg m⁻³)(N kg⁻¹)(m³) = N.
A second way to see the same result is to use the pressure difference from top to bottom, Δp = ρgh, and multiply by area: F = ΔpA = ρghA. Since Ah is the displaced volume, this becomes F = ρgV.

figure.purpose: Model the decision and unit chain for a partly immersed prism.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated worked layout. Left: vertical cylinder crossing an oil surface, with submerged height 0.12 m and area 0.030 m squared. Middle: highlight displaced prism and write V equals Ah. Right: show rho g V substitution, upward direction and unit cancellation.
figure.alt_text: A partly immersed cylinder's submerged height and area are used to find displaced volume and upthrust.

blocks.heading: Floating equilibrium selects its own displaced volume
content: A freely floating object at rest has two vertical forces: weight downward and upthrust upward. Zero resultant force means F = W.
The weight formula to remember is W = mg. For a 75 kg raft floating in fresh water, ρgV = mg. Cancelling g gives V = m/ρ = 75/1000 = 0.075 m³ submerged.

This is a different explanation of floating. If the raft sits too low, it displaces more water, so upthrust grows until it matches weight. If it sits too high, it displaces less water, so weight makes it settle lower.
For a uniform object, write m = ρ_object V_total. Then floating equilibrium gives ρ_fluid V_submerged = ρ_object V_total. The fraction submerged is therefore V_submerged/V_total = ρ_object/ρ_fluid.

symbols: W is weight in newtons, N.
m is mass in kilograms, kg.
g is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram, N kg⁻¹.
formula_to_remember.units: Kilograms multiplied by newtons per kilogram gives newtons.

figure.purpose: Show how a floating object self-adjusts until upthrust equals weight.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper three-state sequence of the same raft: too high with small upward arrow, settling downward, then equilibrium with equal upward F and downward W arrows. Mark the growing shaded displaced volume without adding stability or centre-of-buoyancy ideas.
figure.alt_text: A floating raft settles until its upthrust and weight are equal.

blocks.heading: Deeper does not always mean greater upthrust
content: It is reasonable to think that greater depth must produce greater upthrust because pressure is greater deeper in a liquid. The missing step is that upthrust depends on a pressure difference, not on one pressure value.

For the rigid lunch box in uniform water, moving deeper increases both the top and bottom pressures by the same amount. Their difference stays the same. Its fluid density and displaced volume also stay the same, so F = ρgV stays the same.

A floating object behaves differently when it sinks a little because its submerged volume changes. The larger displaced volume produces a larger upthrust. Ask first whether V changes, not merely whether depth changes.

figure.purpose: Contrast changing absolute pressure with unchanged pressure difference and displaced volume.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison table with shallow and deep fully submerged boxes. Show larger top and bottom pressure arrows in the deep case but equal arrow differences, the same highlighted displaced volume, and equal upward resultant arrows.
figure.alt_text: At greater depth both top and bottom pressures rise, while their difference and the box's upthrust stay unchanged.

blocks.heading: A four-question route through every upthrust problem
content: First ask what fluid is displaced, because its density belongs in ρ. Second identify only the volume below the fluid surface. Third calculate F = ρgV and give the upward direction.

Fourth inspect the other vertical forces. A freely floating object has F = W. A cable, support or extra load adds another force, so draw the forces and use zero resultant force rather than assuming F = W.
Check the result physically. A denser fluid or a larger displaced volume should increase upthrust. For the same floating object, a denser fluid should require a smaller submerged volume.
Stay inside the lesson boundary: these ideas do not yet describe fluid flow, viscous drag or whether a tilted floating object is stable.

figure.purpose: Compress the selection, calculation, force-balance and checking routine.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper four-step flow strip: choose displaced fluid, shade submerged volume, calculate rho g V, then draw vertical force balance. End with two check badges: denser fluid gives more upthrust for fixed V, and denser fluid gives less V for a fixed floating weight.
figure.alt_text: A four-step routine connects displaced fluid, submerged volume, upthrust calculation and vertical equilibrium.

misconceptions_addressed: V in F = ρgV is always the whole object volume.
Every immersed object has upthrust equal to weight.
The object's density is used as ρ in the upthrust formula.
